text: Assume breach only becomes real engineering work once you can put a number on it, and that's what blast radius does. This lesson gives you a precise definition and a repeatable way to estimate it during an architecture review, so it stops being a guess someone makes in a meeting and starts being a documented part of the design.

Blast radius is the maximum scope of damage possible if one specific credential or resource is compromised. Notice what it isn't: it's not a likelihood estimate. How probable compromise is belongs to a different conversation, and it's a conversation people routinely talk themselves out of with optimism. Blast radius skips that argument entirely — it's a structural fact. This service account can reach these resources, that role can write to that storage account, full stop, independent of anyone's guess about whether it will actually happen.

Estimating it means tracing three dimensions that don't move together. Identity reach is what a credential can actually do based on its real permissions, not its intended purpose — a service account scoped to Contributor reaches far more than one scoped to a single storage container. Network reach is what a compromised device can connect to, shaped directly by segmentation. And detection time is how long abnormal use would go unnoticed — a small blast radius that's invisible to logging is still effectively large, because nothing limits how long an attacker gets to operate inside it.

Three patterns consistently grow blast radius without anyone intending it. Golden images and shared VM templates bake the same credential or agent into every instance built from them, so one compromised instance can expose them all. Shared secrets — one API key or connection string used by several applications — multiply blast radius by everything that trusts it. And broadly-scoped IAM roles, the classic "just give it Contributor, it's easier," end up bounded only by the subscription instead of the actual task.

None of this matters unless it gets written down. A blast-radius estimate has to be an artifact attached to the design — what can this reach today, is that reach actually required, and how would we detect abnormal use of it — not something reasoned about once and forgotten. Next lesson takes the identity and network side of this further, into the specific techniques attackers actually use to move laterally once they have a foothold, and the controls built specifically to stop each one.
